title: Replace a worn wiper blade on a spring-loaded J-hook arm, holding the arm up and lowering it gently onto the glass
instruction: Replace the wiper blade with the new one and lay the arm back on the windshield.
context: Most drivers have changed a wiper blade or watched it done at an auto-parts counter. A wiper arm is sprung against the glass at about 8 N and does not stay up: let go, it snaps back, and a bare hook or a slammed blade can chip or crack a windshield. One hand must hold the arm up against its spring while the other presses the adapter's release tab, slides the old blade toward the pivot out of the hook's bend and draws it off; then the new blade's adapter must be brought up under the hook behind the bend, lined up with the arm, and pulled toward the bend until it clicks, in that order. Finally the arm is lowered by hand onto the glass, not dropped.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, on the table top (x forward, y left). Windshield: clear 5 mm acrylic sheet, 68 cm wide (y) x 36 cm up the slope, sloping up away from the arms at 27 deg: lower edge top surface at x 20, z 3, centred on y -2, upper edge at x 52, z 19, on a black front rail and a rear block fixed to the table. Wiper arm: black steel J-hook arm (9x4 hook: 9 mm wide, 2.5 mm strip bent round the adapter), 300 g, pivot post on the glass 11 cm up the slope at y -32, hinge axis 4.9 cm above the glass along the slope; lies across the glass toward +y, hook 36 cm from the pivot (y +4). Spring: 8 N on the glass at the blade centre; does not stay up; stop at 45 deg; bare, it rests on its hook on the glass. Old blade: worn 18 in (45 cm) conventional blade, dull grey frame, 110 g, 2.4 cm tall, its J-hook adapter (30x11x10 mm) latched in the hook; release tab (10x16 mm lever on the adapter's side facing the arms) frees the latch when pressed 1.5 mm (about 5 N). New blade: same model, black frame, adapter fitted, standing on its rubber in a cardboard tray (48x4 cm, 12 mm slot, walls 12 mm tall) at x 33, y 45, running along x, adapter nose toward the arms. Nothing else on the table; arms in the ready pose.
scoring: 0 if at any time: the arm lands on the glass with the hook faster than 0.75 m/s (a fall of about 3 cm on its spring; real trial: video shows it let go 3 cm or more up or snapping down); the bare hook touches the glass (video); a latched blade is forced off the hook (photo: hook bent / adapter broken, or blade off without the tab pressed); a blade falls off the table. Otherwise: 0.25 old blade off the hook, lying on the table (lowest point within 1.5 cm of the table, not on the windshield or stand) and let go (photo); 0.5 and the new blade latched in the hook (adapter in the bend; after the trial a 2 kg pull along the arm does not move it); 0.75 and the arm resting on the glass on the new blade (hinge within -0.6 to +1 deg of rest, still; photo: rubber on the glass along its length); 1.0 and every gripper 3 cm or more from the arm and both blades, held 1 s (video). Re-latching the old blade or leaving it on the windshield scores 0.
reset_notes: Lift the arm, hook the worn blade back on (adapter clicked) and lower the arm onto the glass; stand the new blade, adapter clicked in its J-hook position, back in the tray slot on its mark. Nothing is used up. If a hook was bent or an adapter broken (a scored failure), replace that part.
fidelity: Approximate. Rigid boxes; rigid blade on a flat panel. Arm: one hinge with an implicit spring (2.9 N m at rest). The hook is drawn without a collider: a state machine switches D6 joints between blade and arm (weld when latched; 16 mm slide along the arm when threaded). The tab is a real sprung part; the latch needs the tab pressed and a 13 mm push to release, and engages only from behind the bend, lined up within 3 mm and 6 deg, with up to 7 N to click.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo: 1.0 (seed 0; also 1.0 on seeds 4 and 10)
